source.title: Large Language Model Federated Learning with Blockchain and Unlearning for Cross-Organizational Collaboration
source.authors: Xuhan Zuo; Ming-Hao Wang; Tian-Qing Zhu; Shui Yu; Wan-Lei Zhou

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates a LoRA-based data-forgetting procedure using post-unlearning accuracy, but does not use the recovery attacks or unlearning methods named in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports accuracy before and after LoRA unlearning on IMDB and Twitter and compares selected results with retraining from scratch. It does not test recovery by fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, or prompting. It does not state a chance baseline or report a separate measure of retained general ability, so the reported accuracies do not establish the full Version A condition.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a LoRA-based unlearning step inside a blockchain federated-learning framework. It reports only its own method's accuracy drop on IMDB and Twitter, plus a retrain-from-scratch comparison. It runs no recovery attack (fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, prompting). It reports no retained or general-ability accuracy and states no chance level. So none of versions A–F is tested; this is a method-performance report.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors claim their tuned LoRA unlearning removes target data while keeping performance on the remaining data, matches retraining from scratch in final accuracy, and is computationally cheaper. They also claim the hybrid blockchain adds little overhead. No reported number backs the claim of preserved performance on the remaining data. No unlearning-versus-retraining timing is reported either: Table IV times only the federated-learning and blockchain overhead. The healthcare and education case studies are descriptive and report no results.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes LoRA-based adapter updates for forgetting specified data; it does not test gradient ascent, Who's Harry Potter, RMU, or the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that the results vary with LoRA rank, alpha, and dropout; higher ranks, lower alpha values, and higher dropout rates generally yield larger accuracy reductions.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA-based unlearning drops classification accuracy from about 74–99% to about 1–9% on IMDB and Twitter, similar to retraining from scratch. Larger rank, lower alpha and higher dropout give larger drops.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LoRA adapter unlearning on classification tasks reduces accuracy on the target data about as much as retraining, with size depending on LoRA hyperparameters. Neither retained ability nor robustness is measured.

record.problems: The paper gives no model name or size, chance baseline, uncertainty estimates, or separate evaluation on retained/general data. The reported accuracy reductions therefore do not show whether targeted knowledge reached chance while general ability was preserved.

untested.parts: Near-chance targeted accuracy (no chance level stated; binary-task values near 1% are below chance), preservation of general ability (not reported), and robustness to simple attacks (not tested).
No relearning or fine-tuning recovery test.
No activation ablation and no analysis of access-blocking versus deletion.
No prompting, rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery test.
The method is not evaluated against any recovery attack.

record.verdict_notes: What changed from the earlier verdict: (1) The merge refused the earlier verdict because of the record's top-level version list (V1–V6), which a verdict cannot edit directly. I mapped those IDs by what the reader's untested_parts describe, not by position: V1 = A (post-unlearning accuracy, chance level, retained ability, attacks), V2 = B (fine-tuning recovery), V3 = C (activation ablation or access-blocking analysis), V4 = D (quantization), V5 = E (prompt, language or in-context recovery), V6 = F (the method's robustness to those attacks). The untested list already covers all six declared IDs A–F. (2) I re-checked each row's link from what it measures. Each of r1–r14 is a single post-unlearning classification accuracy on IMDB or Twitter for an unnamed model. Algorithm 7 evaluates on a validation set that the paper does not split into forget and retained data, and there is no attack. So no row measures A's construct (targeted knowledge near chance with general ability kept) or anything in B–F. All rows stay at none / cannot_determine, and the reader's V1 tag is not carried over as A. (3) authors_conclusion now also says that the efficiency claim against retraining has no reported timing, and that the case studies report no results. Everything else from the earlier verdict is kept: relation, tranche, test_reason, row problems, untested, fits_no_version and empty labels/missing. Points kept from earlier notes: sub-chance accuracies (about 1%) on binary IMDB suggest the model was driven to wrong labels rather than to forgetting. The model, its size, the forget-set definition and uncertainty are all unreported. This is a blockchain/federated-learning framework paper in which unlearning is one component. It cites Eldan & Russinovich (an original) only in related work. The study is not an original, so rule 6 does not apply. The text contains no instructions to the reader.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports accuracy after unlearning but does not establish a chance baseline, separately evaluate performance on retained/general data, or test whether attacks recover the data.
No post-unlearning recovery by fine-tuning is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of access-blocking versus deletion is tested.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
The method is not evaluated against the attacks above.

The model is unnamed, and it is unclear whether accuracy is on the forget set or the whole validation set.
